title: Work and live
hookLine: doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years (Isha Upanishad 2)
tomorrow: could you see yourself in someone you can't stand?

lines: VERSE TWO: WORK, AND LIVE LONG.
cards: One video says quit everything and go find yourself. The next says grind harder. The Isha Upanishad seems to say both, one verse apart.
Verse one: enjoy the world by letting it go. Verse two: doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. Thus, and not otherwise, action does not cling to you.
So which is it? Drop it all, or work and want a long life? That's the odd detail, and a king who plowed his own field helps solve it.

teach.b: Valmiki's Ramayana says King Janaka of Mithila was plowing a field when he found a baby girl in the furrow, and raised her as his daughter: Sita. A king, behind a plow.

teach.h: IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.
teach.b: The Mahabharata gives the same Janaka this line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. He ran a whole kingdom and didn't belong to it.
And in the Gita, Krishna names Janaka as one who reached perfection through action itself. Now the puzzle. Teachers have read verse two two ways.
The commentator Shankara read it as a second path, for those not yet ready to give everything up for knowledge.

Others, close to the Gita, read verse two as the way to do verse one: you let go not by leaving your work but inside it. For anyone living by verse two, the teaching is what the Gita calls karma yoga.
Action itself doesn't bind you. Clinging does.
Do the work, want the long life, and hold the results the way Janaka held his city. The verse's own words: thus, and not otherwise.
For Shankara the forest path still stands beside it; for those other readers, the way is through the work.

how: Hindus read the Isha's second verse alongside the Bhagavad Gita's teaching of karma yoga, action done without clinging to its fruits, and teachers have read its fit with the first verse in more than one way.

o: rest now, because work keeps you from living
do your work fully here, and want a long life
live a hundred years by working without a break

games.q: the king and the verse: tap the pairs.
p: a king who found Sita in a furrow
his city: if it burns, nothing of mine
read verse two as a second path

s: the Isha says the spiritual life means leaving your work behind
verse two says do your work here and wish to live a hundred years: thus, and not otherwise.
the Gita names King Janaka as one who reached perfection through action
Krishna points to Janaka and others who got there by action itself.
all Hindu teachers read the Isha's second verse the same way
Shankara read it as a second path; others read it as the way to live the first verse.

games.q: you love your job but it eats you alive. a friend says the spiritual move is to quit. what does the Isha's second verse suggest?
o: keep doing the work, and drop the clinging; action doesn't bind, clinging does.
quit; verse one says let everything go, so work is the obstacle.
work harder; the verse promises a hundred years to whoever does the most.
games.why: thus, and not otherwise: the verse keeps the work and changes the grip. Janaka ran a kingdom and didn't belong to it.

practice: Stand up and walk, slowly, to wherever today's work waits for you: a desk, a sink, a laptop, a door. Feel each step as part of the work, not a delay before it. When you arrive, rest a hand on it for a breath, and begin.

wordCard.voice: Work and live: the Isha's second verse, kurvann eveha karmani, doing your work right here, you may wish to live a hundred years.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Isha Upanishad 2: doing works here.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: work and live, through the work, not around it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 2 (doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years; thus and not otherwise; action does not cling to a person)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 66 (Janaka finds Sita while plowing the field)
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Janaka: when Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns)
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (Janaka and others attained perfection by action)
